title: Spectral Energy Shifts in Graph Anomaly Detection
one_liner: Detect hidden anomalies in networks by measuring where energy concentrates, not just how much it swings.
lead: A graph is a network of connected points where messages flow between nodes. Most anomaly detectors look for points acting wildly different — but some sneaky anomalies hide by pretending to be normal while subtly shifting where the network's energy sits. This paper finds those hidden anomalies by tracking how energy spreads across nodes, which older methods miss.

problem.h2: The blind spot in anomaly detection
paras: In a network where each point sends messages to its neighbors, some points break and send strange signals. Most detection methods catch these noisy points easily. But some broken points are sneaky: they send just the right signals to look normal in total volume, while secretly shifting where the energy pools.

Existing detectors only check if the total energy got louder or softer. If an anomaly keeps the volume the same but reshuffles it, the detector walks right past it. A beginner might measure total signal strength and declare the network healthy — but that is like checking if a room is warm without noticing the heat is all in one corner.

callout.html: Catch anomalies by watching where network energy concentrates, not just how strong it is overall.

steps.text: For each point, measure how strong its received signals are
Remember which nodes hold high vs low energy in the network
Notice when energy moves from one node cluster to another
Send this shift information through the network so neighbors react
Catch points that hide by rearranging energy without changing total

paras: The paper rewrites how the network measures itself. Instead of just summing all signals into one number, it tracks how energy spreads across individual nodes and whether that spread changes. This one change — measuring per-node distribution instead of total volume — lets the detector see anomalies that rearrange without shouting.

hidden.name: Energy concentration pattern
paras: The hidden quantity is spectral energy shift — a measure of where the network's signal power sits in any given moment. Spectral energy means the strength of different patterns that emerge when you listen to the whole network together. If that pattern changes shape, something changed even if the total stayed the same.

The paper estimates this by looking at each node's contribution to the overall signal pattern. It compares node-by-node energy in the current moment to node-by-node energy in a normal baseline. A big shift in how the energy is spread out (even if the sum stays constant) reveals a camouflaged anomaly.

heat.caption: Darker nodes hold more energy; marked nodes shifted unexpectedly from baseline

reads.html: Energy concentration: how much signal power pools in individual nodes versus spreading evenly
Node-level spectral energy: the contribution of each node to the dominant patterns in the graph's signal strength across time

mechanism.h2: Why shifting energy reveals hidden anomalies
paras: A camouflaged anomaly sends signals carefully crafted so the total looks normal. But it must get those signals from somewhere — it cannot create energy, only move it. So it drains energy from some neighbors and floods others. That reshuffling leaves a footprint: the distribution of who has strong signals changes shape.

The paper catches this by watching not just total power but the pattern of which nodes are loud. Message passing (the standard way graphs learn) naturally spreads information node-to-node. When you teach the network to pass information about energy shifts (not just energy values), the network learns to notice when neighbors are rearranging unusually. A node detecting an anomaly neighbor sees its own energy pattern deviate from what it should be given the incoming messages.

Why this works: normal nodes follow predictable rules about how energy flows between neighbors. An anomaly breaks those rules by moving energy in a way that a normal flow would not. Measuring distribution shift directly exposes that rule-breaking, even when the anomaly keeps the total volume hidden.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose node A normally gets energy [20, 30, 50] from three neighbor channels.
Today it gets energy [25, 10, 65] — same total (120) but shifted.
This node's high score (650) flags it as anomalous.
A truly normal node with [21,29,50] gives distance 1² + 1² + 0² = 2 (low score, passes).

math.note: The paper measures which nodes shift their energy pattern furthest from normal, catching anomalies that hide by rearranging instead of changing total volume.

items.html: If the baseline pattern is contaminated with anomalies, the detector learns to tolerate them. Anomalies must be rare enough that baseline calculation ignores them.
If the network's normal behavior slowly changes over time, the distribution shifts gradually. The detector needs a moving baseline, not a fixed one, to stay calibrated.

items.b: Coordinated shifting is hard to spot.
items.html: If many nodes shift together in a coordinated way, the collective pattern might still look normal even though individuals changed. Detecting group anomalies requires tracking correlations, not just per-node shifts.

items.b: Works best when normal is truly steady.
items.html: The method excels when normal networks have predictable energy distributions. Set a clean baseline, update it as the network evolves, and measure deviations from it.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small network with five nodes. Run normal traffic for 100 steps to establish baseline energy patterns. Inject a camouflaged anomaly at node 3: send signals that keep total energy flat but concentrate all power into node 3 for 20 steps. Run a naive detector (total energy threshold) and this paper's detector (distribution shift threshold) side by side. The naive detector should miss it. This paper's detector should flag node 3.
demo.metric_eq: Detection score = (camouflaged anomalies caught + normal nodes passed) / (camouflaged anomalies + normal nodes)
demo.closing: The demo proves the catch: distribution shift catches hidden anomalies because anomalies rearrange energy across nodes instead of shouting louder overall, and watching per-node patterns exposes that rearrangement while total-volume methods miss it.
